learn.intro: The Liberal governments of 1906–11 took new responsibility for people's health. Then the First World War created terrible wounds — and pushed forward surgery, X-rays, blood transfusion and the role of women in medicine.

blocks.p: Why? Surveys by Charles Booth (London) and Seebohm Rowntree (York) showed that about a third of people lived in poverty. During the Boer War (1899–1902) many volunteers were rejected as unfit, worrying the government about national strength. The new Labour Party competed for working-class votes, and Liberal politicians such as David Lloyd George and Winston Churchill wanted reform.

ul: 1906: free school meals for poor children.
1907: school medical inspections — the School Medical Service.
1911: National Insurance Act — workers paid in to receive sick pay and free treatment from a doctor (but not their families).

blocks.p: Impact: the government accepted responsibility for health and welfare, children's health improved, and some sick workers were protected. But wives, children and the unemployed were often left out, and hospital treatment was not covered.

sections.title: 2. The First World War: surgery and treatment

blocks.p: Trench warfare caused huge numbers of wounds from shells and bullets, often infected by soil bacteria (gas gangrene). Doctors developed debridement (cutting away dead tissue), and Carrel–Dakin solution to irrigate wounds.
The Thomas splint kept broken legs still and greatly reduced deaths from fractures of the thigh bone. Harold Gillies pioneered plastic surgery to rebuild faces at Queen's Hospital, Sidcup (1917).
X-rays: mobile X-ray units — including those organised by Marie Curie — found bullets and shrapnel near the front line.
Blood transfusion: adding sodium citrate stopped blood clotting, so blood could be stored. In 1917 a blood depot was set up before the Battle of Cambrai.

evidence: Thomas splint reduced deaths from thigh fractures.
1917: Gillies at Sidcup; blood stored before Cambrai.

sections.title: 3. The war and women in medicine

blocks.p: Thousands of women served as nurses, including volunteers in the Voluntary Aid Detachments (VADs) and the First Aid Nursing Yeomanry (FANY), who drove ambulances. Women doctors such as Elsie Inglis set up the Scottish Women's Hospitals, which worked in France and Serbia, after the War Office initially refused her help.
The war showed women's skill and courage, and more medical schools admitted women — though many restrictions returned after 1918.

evidence: Elsie Inglis and the Scottish Women's Hospitals.

timeline.event: Gillies opens Queen's Hospital, Sidcup; blood stored before Cambrai

matching.title: Match the wartime development to its purpose

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of Liberal public health measures.
evidence.model: Free school meals (1906), school medical inspections (1907), old-age pensions (1908), National Insurance (1911).

flashcards.q: Give three reasons for the Liberal reforms.
flashcards.a: Booth and Rowntree's surveys; unfit Boer War recruits; competition from Labour; reforming Liberal politicians.

flashcards.q: What were the limits of National Insurance?
flashcards.a: Only insured workers; not families, the unemployed or hospital treatment.

flashcards.q: How did the war improve treatment of infected wounds?
flashcards.a: Debridement and Carrel–Dakin solution to irrigate wounds.
Sodium citrate stopped clotting, so blood could be stored and given to wounded soldiers quickly.

flashcards.q: How did the war affect women in medicine?
flashcards.a: Nurses, VADs, FANY drivers, women doctors like Elsie Inglis showed their abilities; more medical schools admitted women.

checklist.text: I can explain the reasons for and impact on public health of the Liberal reforms (1906–11).
I can explain how the First World War improved surgery, X-rays, blood transfusion and fighting infection.
I can describe the importance of the First World War for women in medicine.
